algebraic-cage-bounds.title: Match the range for n
algebraic-cage-bounds.note: Find the n−4 cage at R1C4 and the n+2 cage in row 3.

steps.title: Use the one-cell cage
steps.description: R1C4 can contain 1 through 4. Its total is n−4, so n can be 5 through 8.

steps.title: Check the two-cell cage
steps.description: The two largest distinct digits are 3 and 4. Their sum is 7, so n+2 is at most 7. That puts n at 5 or less.

steps.title: Use the value both cages allow
steps.description: Only n = 5 meets both bounds. Then n−4 equals 1. Place 1 in R1C4.

algebraic-cage-practice.title: Find the candidate to remove
algebraic-cage-practice.note: Compare the m−2 cage at R2C1 with the m+2 cage in row 4.

steps.title: Start with the highest two-cell total
steps.description: Use the greatest possible sum for the m+2 cage to bound the digit in R2C1.

diagram-key.title: Reading the marks
diagram-key.note: Use the row and column labels to find a cell. This diagram shows how the app marks each step.

steps.title: Find a candidate
steps.description: R2C4 means row 2, column 4. The small 5 in the center is one possible digit. The ring marks it for this step.

steps.title: Compare the groups
steps.description: Blue marks the first group and amber marks the second. Both are still possibilities.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.description: A red strike marks a removal and a green ring marks a placement. During a trial, both apply only to that trial.

candidate-elimination.title: A pair leaves one choice
candidate-elimination.note: These three cells in row 3 show their full candidate lists.

steps.title: Find the pair
steps.description: R3C4 and R3C5 each allow only 2 and 8. Because they share row 3, they must hold one of each.

steps.title: Remove 2 and 8 from R3C6
steps.description: The pair supplies both digits to row 3. Its order makes no difference to R3C6.

steps.title: Place 5
steps.description: After those two removals, only 5 remains in R3C6.

weak-link.title: A dashed link rules out a pair of placements
weak-link.note: In row 4, A is R4C2 and B is R4C5. A third possible 5 is in R4C8.

steps.title: At most one end is true
steps.description: A and B share row 4, so they cannot both be 5. Both can be false if the 5 goes in R4C8.

steps.title: Suppose A is 5
steps.description: A 5 in R4C2 rules out 5 in R4C5 and R4C8. The arrow points from the assumption toward its consequence.

steps.title: Suppose A loses 5
steps.description: Row 4 still has two places for 5, R4C5 and R4C8. Removing A leaves B undecided.

strong-link.title: A solid link needs at least one true end
strong-link.note: This time row 4 has exactly two possible places for 5, R4C2 and R4C8.

steps.title: Find both places
steps.description: Row 4 must contain 5, so at least one end of the solid link is true. The row also prevents both from being true.

steps.title: Suppose A loses 5
steps.description: If R4C2 cannot be 5, row 4 forces 5 into R4C8.

steps.title: Use the same pair in the other direction
steps.description: If R4C2 is 5, row 4 rules out 5 in R4C8. The dashed link shows this conflict.

wing-cases.title: Both pivot choices rule out 9
wing-cases.note: R1C1 is the pivot. Its wings are A at R1C4 and B at R4C1. The target is R4C4.

steps.title: Read the pivot
steps.description: R1C1 allows only 2 or 6. Its 2 sees the 2 in wing A along row 1. Its 6 sees the 6 in wing B down column 1.

steps.title: Suppose the pivot is 2
steps.description: Row 1 rules out 2 in A, so A must be 9. Column 4 then rules out 9 in R4C4.

steps.title: Suppose the pivot is 6
steps.description: Column 1 rules out 6 in B, so B must be 9. Row 4 then rules out 9 in R4C4.

steps.title: Use the result of both cases
steps.description: Both choices remove 9 from R4C4, leaving 5. You can place that 5 while R1C1 still has two choices.

uniqueness-swap.title: Two ways to fill four cells
uniqueness-swap.note: All four cells began empty. The large digits show possible completions.

steps.title: Fill the first diagonal with 1
steps.description: Each of the two rows, two columns, and two boxes now has one 1 and one 7 in these cells.

steps.title: Exchange the 1s and 7s
steps.description: Each house still contains the same two digits. If the first arrangement solves the classic puzzle, the second solves it too.

chain-walk.title: Trace four possible 5s
chain-walk.note: Rows 1 and 4 each have only two places for 5. The diagram shows the 5s used in the proof.

steps.title: Read the four ends
steps.description: A is R1C1, B is R1C5, C is R4C5, and D is R4C2. The path reads A = B - C = D.

steps.title: Suppose A is false
steps.description: For this trial, suppose R1C1 cannot be 5. Leave the pencil mark on your own board.

steps.title: Row 1 forces B
steps.description: Only A and B can supply row 1 with 5. Without A, B must be 5.

steps.title: Column 5 rules out C
steps.description: If R1C5 is 5, R4C5 cannot also be 5 in column 5.

steps.title: Row 4 forces D
steps.description: Without 5 in R4C5, the only place for 5 in row 4 is R4C2. Ruling out A forces D.

steps.title: Remove 5 from R2C2
steps.description: A or D must be 5. R2C2 sees A in box 1 and D in column 2, so either one rules out its 5.

cell-link.title: A chain can switch digits inside a cell
cell-link.note: R6C4 allows only 2 and 7. Each candidate is a separate end of the link.

steps.title: Read (2=7)r6c4
steps.description: The equals sign marks a strong link inside R6C4. At least one of its two candidates must be true.

steps.title: Suppose 2 is false
steps.description: With 2 gone, R6C4 must be 7. The chain can continue from 7.

steps.title: Suppose 2 is true
steps.description: R6C4 has room for one digit. If it is 2, it cannot also be 7. A dashed line shows that weak link.

als-count.title: Two cells with three possible digits
als-count.note: R6C4 and R6C5 share row 6. Compare three separate trials, one for each missing digit.

steps.title: Count 1, 4, and 8 once each
steps.description: These two cells must use two different digits from {1, 4, 8}. Exactly one digit is absent from the pair.

steps.title: Suppose both cells lose 1
steps.description: R6C4 must be 4. Row 6 then rules out 4 in R6C5, leaving 8.

steps.title: Suppose both cells lose 4
steps.description: R6C4 must be 1 and R6C5 must be 8. Both possible 4s must disappear for this case.

steps.title: Suppose both cells lose 8
steps.description: R6C5 must be 4, so R6C4 must be 1. The original lists allow all three trials.

grouped-link.title: Two places count as one end of a link
grouped-link.note: In row 3, G means that R3C1 or R3C2 contains 5. Amber marks both places.

steps.title: Read (5)r3c12
steps.description: The solid link ends at the whole amber group. The notation gives one digit, one row, and two possible columns.

steps.title: Rule out one member
steps.description: If R3C1 loses 5, the group still has R3C2. Row 3 does not yet force 5 into R3C8.

steps.title: Rule out both members
steps.description: If neither amber cell can be 5, row 3 has just one place left. R3C8 must be 5.

rcc-link.title: A digit that cannot appear in both sets
rcc-link.note: Blue marks two cells with {1, 4, 6} between them. Amber marks two cells with {2, 6, 7}.

steps.title: Find every 6 in row 8
steps.description: The three possible 6s all share row 8. A 6 in either set rules out every 6 in the other.

steps.title: Suppose R8C5 is 6
steps.description: Row 8 rules out both blue 6s. The two blue cells must now use 1 and 4.

steps.title: Suppose neither set uses 6
steps.description: Blue must use 1 and 4. Amber must use 2 and 7. This also satisfies the weak link.

steps.title: Add a possible 6 in R9C6
steps.description: The blue 6s cannot see this new amber 6. Both sets can now use 6 without a conflict between those places.

contradiction.title: A trial that puts two 2s in column 1
contradiction.note: The four cells show all their candidates. Keep the trial moves separate from the original grid.

steps.title: Pick the candidate to test
steps.description: Can R1C1 be 2? The other three cells each have just two choices.

steps.title: Suppose R1C1 is 2
steps.description: Row 1 rules out 2 in R1C4. Its only remaining candidate is 5.

steps.title: Follow the two forced cells
steps.description: Column 4 rules out 5 in R4C4, leaving 8. Row 4 then rules out 8 in R4C1, leaving 2.

steps.title: Find the conflict
steps.description: The trial puts 2 in both R1C1 and R4C1. Column 1 allows only one 2.

steps.title: Return to the original grid
steps.description: Remove 2 from R1C1. Its only remaining digit is 9. The other moves depended on the failed trial.

nested-branches.title: A trial inside another trial
nested-branches.note: Each arrow stands for a sequence of moves. Read the inner branches before returning to the outer choice.

steps.title: Keep the outer assumption
steps.description: Suppose A is true. Whether B is true or false, C follows. You can use C in the A branch.

children.result: A proved deduction leads to C.
A proved deduction also leads to C.

branches.result: Not checked. C is still unknown in this branch.

steps.title: Compare both outer cases
steps.description: Now suppose A is false. If this case also forces C, you can use C on the original grid.

children.result: A proved deduction leads to C.
A proved deduction also leads to C.

branches.result: A separate proof reaches C here too.

seeing-cells.title: Which cells see the 5?
seeing-cells.note: The large 5 is a placed digit. Each small 5 is a candidate.

steps.title: Start in R2C2
steps.description: R2C2 contains 5. Find the other cells in its row, its column, and its box.

steps.title: Look across row 2
steps.description: R2C4 shares row 2 with R2C2, so remove 5 from R2C4.

steps.title: Look down column 2
steps.description: R4C2 shares column 2 with R2C2, so remove 5 from R4C2.

steps.title: Look inside box 1
steps.description: R3C3 shares box 1 with R2C2 and loses 5. R4C4 shares no house with R2C2, so keep its candidate.

subset-count.title: Three cells reserve three digits
subset-count.note: The four marked cells show their complete candidate lists in row 4.

steps.title: Read the three blue cells
steps.description: The lists in R4C1, R4C2, and R4C4 contain just three different digits, 2, 4, and 7.

steps.title: Use the row rule
steps.description: Row 4 cannot repeat a digit. Its three blue cells must use one 2, one 4, and one 7.

steps.title: Look at R4C6
steps.description: The three blue cells supply the 2 and the 7 for row 4. Remove both from R4C6. Only 1 remains.

fish-count.title: Three rows need three columns
fish-count.note: The rings show every possible 5 in rows 3, 5, and 7. The candidate to test is in row 4.

steps.title: Count the rows
steps.description: Each of the three marked rows needs its own 5.

steps.title: Count the columns
steps.description: The six possible places all lie in columns 3, 4, and 7. Each of the three rows must use a different one.

steps.title: Test 5 in R4C4
steps.description: A 5 here uses column 4. That leaves only columns 3 and 7 for the three marked rows. Remove 5 from R4C4.

coloring-states.title: Two colors for the possible 5s
coloring-states.note: Each solid line joins the only two possible 5s in a row or column.

steps.title: Color the pair in row 2
steps.description: Exactly one of R2C2 and R2C5 is 5. Color one blue and the other amber.

steps.title: Continue from R2C5
steps.description: Column 5 makes R4C5 blue. Row 4 then makes R4C3 amber.

steps.title: Try blue
steps.description: R2C2 would contain 5. Box 1 then rules out 5 in R3C3.

steps.title: Try amber
steps.description: R4C3 would contain 5. Column 3 then rules out 5 in R3C3.

steps.title: Remove 5 from R3C3
steps.description: One color must be true. Each color rules out the same 5 in R3C3.

loop-matching-links.title: Two matching links at the join
loop-matching-links.note: The first three steps show a weak-link join. The last two use a different grid with a strong-link join.

steps.title: Find the two weak links
steps.description: A is the 5 in R3C2. Row 2 needs a 5 in B at R2C1 or C at R2C3. A sees both in box 1.

steps.title: Suppose A is true
steps.description: A rules out B. Row 2 then forces C. C rules out A in box 1.

steps.title: Remove the 5 at A
steps.description: The trial both uses and rules out 5 in R3C2. Remove that 5.

steps.title: Find the two strong links
steps.description: A is now R2C2. Row 2 links it to B. Column 2 links it to C. B and C see each other in box 1.

steps.title: Suppose A is false
steps.description: Row 2 forces B, which rules out C in box 1. Column 2 then forces A. This contradiction proves that A must be 5.

loop-alternating-links.title: A loop with alternating links at every cell
loop-alternating-links.note: R4C1 and R4C2 both allow only 2 and 7. Look at the links inside the cells and along row 4.

steps.title: Choose the weak link between the 7s
steps.description: The two cells share row 4, so at most one of the two 7s is true.

steps.title: Go around the other way
steps.description: If R4C1 loses 7, it must be 2. Row 4 rules out 2 in R4C2, so R4C2 must be 7.

steps.title: Remove 7 from R4C4
steps.description: One end of the link must contain 7. Either end supplies row 4 with its 7, so R4C4 cannot be 7.

als-link.title: A strong link between two digits in a set
als-link.note: R6C4 and R6C5 have three digits between them. The link refers to the two cells together.

steps.title: Locate the 1 and both 4s
steps.description: Blue marks the possible 1. Amber marks both places where the set can use 4.

steps.title: Suppose the set misses 1
steps.description: R6C4 must be 4, so R6C5 must be 8. The set uses 4.

steps.title: Suppose the set misses 4
steps.description: Remove 4 from both cells in this trial. R6C4 must be 1 and R6C5 must be 8.

steps.title: Try 1 and 4 together
steps.description: R6C4 can be 1 while R6C5 is 4. Both ends of this strong link can be true.

placement-capacity.title: Four cells need four slots
placement-capacity.note: The blue cells show all their candidates. R1C5 is outside the group.

steps.title: Count the slots
steps.description: Every candidate in the four blue cells uses at least one of the four listed slots. Each slot can supply only one cell.

steps.title: Try 1 in R1C1
steps.description: This 1 uses both the row 1 slot and the column 1 slot. Only two slots remain for three blue cells.

steps.title: Try 1 in R1C5
steps.description: This outside placement uses a slot in row 1. The four blue cells then have only three slots left.

complete-digit-layouts.title: Two ways to finish placing the 5s
complete-digit-layouts.note: Six 5s are outside the diagram. Rows 1, 2, and 3 still need 5s, as do columns 2, 5, and 8.

steps.title: Mark the remaining places
steps.description: Each of the three rows needs one 5. Each of the three boxes across the top also needs one.

steps.title: Try 5 in R3C5
steps.description: Rows 1 and 2 then both need column 2 for their 5. A column cannot contain two 5s.

steps.title: Put 5 in R1C2 and R2C5
steps.description: A 5 in R3C8 completes the layout. Each row, column, and box has one 5.

steps.title: Put 5 in R1C5 and R2C2
steps.description: R3C8 completes this layout too. The 5s in rows 1 and 2 use different columns than before.

steps.title: Compare both layouts
steps.description: Both put 5 in R3C8, so place it there. Neither puts 5 in R3C5, so remove that candidate.
